steps.narration: Every time you type a website name, a quiet system called DNS turns it into a number your computer can actually use.
Let's see how that lookup happens, step by step.
Computers find each other using IP addresses, strings of numbers like ninety three dot one eight four dot two one five dot one four.
People, on the other hand, are much better at remembering names like example dot com.
The Domain Name System, or DNS, is the shared directory that maps one to the other.
Your browser asks: what is the address for example dot com?
The question goes to a resolver, usually run by your internet provider, which does the legwork for you.
The resolver asks a root server, which points it to the servers for dot com.
The dot com servers point it to the name servers that are responsible for example dot com.
Finally the authoritative server answers with the real IP address, and the resolver hands it back to your browser.
On a first visit, the resolver may need several round trips across the internet.
Next time, the answer is already cached, so it comes back almost instantly.
An uncached lookup can take tens of milliseconds.
Cached answers are kept until their time to live, or T T L, runs out.
There are just thirteen named root server identities.

steps.text: served by over a thousand machines worldwide
steps.narration: But each one is copied across many locations, so well over a thousand machines answer root queries around the world.

steps.text: DNS turns names into IP addresses
steps.narration: To recap: DNS turns names into IP addresses.
Resolvers walk from the root, to the top level domain, to the authoritative server.
And caching makes the whole thing fast enough that you never notice it happening.
